verses.text: There happened to be there a base fellow, whose name was Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjamite; and he blew the trumpet, and said, “We have no portion in David, neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse. Every man to his tents, Israel!”
So all the men of Israel went up from following David, and followed Sheba the son of Bichri; but the men of Judah joined with their king, from the Jordan even to Jerusalem.

David came to his house at Jerusalem; and the king took the ten women his concubines, whom he had left to keep the house, and put them in custody, and provided them with sustenance, but didn’t go in to them. So they were shut up to the day of their death, living in widowhood.
Then the king said to Amasa, “Call me the men of Judah together within three days, and be here present.”
So Amasa went to call the men of Judah together; but he stayed longer than the set time which he had appointed him.

David said to Abishai, “Now Sheba the son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom did. Take your lord’s servants, and pursue after him, lest he get himself fortified cities, and escape out of our sight.”
Joab’s men went out after him, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and all the mighty men; and they went out of Jerusalem, to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.

When they were at the great stone which is in Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Joab was clothed in his apparel of war that he had put on, and on it was a sash with a sword fastened on his waist in its sheath; and as he went along it fell out.
Joab said to Amasa, “Is it well with you, my brother?” Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him.

But Amasa took no heed to the sword that was in Joab’s hand. So he struck him with it in the body, and shed out his bowels to the ground, and didn’t strike him again; and he died. Joab and Abishai his brother pursued Sheba the son of Bichri.
One of Joab’s young men stood by him, and said, “He who favors Joab, and he who is for David, let him follow Joab!”

Amasa lay wallowing in his blood in the middle of the highway. When the man saw that all the people stood still, he carried Amasa out of the highway into the field, and cast a garment over him, when he saw that everyone who came by him stood still.
When he was removed out of the highway, all the people went on after Joab, to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.
He went through all the tribes of Israel to Abel, and to Beth Maacah, and all the Berites. They were gathered together, and went also after him.

They came and besieged him in Abel of Beth Maacah, and they cast up a mound against the city, and it stood against the rampart; and all the people who were with Joab battered the wall, to throw it down.
Then a wise woman cried out of the city, “Hear, hear! Please say to Joab, ‘Come near here, that I may speak with you.’”
He came near to her; and the woman said, “Are you Joab?” He answered, “I am.” Then she said to him, “Hear the words of your servant.” He answered, “I’m listening.”
Then she spoke, saying, “They used to say in old times, ‘They shall surely ask counsel at Abel;’ and so they settled a matter.
I am among those who are peaceable and faithful in Israel. You seek to destroy a city and a mother in Israel. Why will you swallow up Yahweh’s inheritance?”
Joab answered, “Far be it, far be it from me, that I should swallow up or destroy.

The matter is not so. But a man of the hill country of Ephraim, Sheba the son of Bichri by name, has lifted up his hand against the king, even against David. Just deliver him, and I will depart from the city.” The woman said to Joab, “Behold, his head will be thrown to you over the wall.”

Then the woman went to all the people in her wisdom. They cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri, and threw it out to Joab. He blew the trumpet, and they were dispersed from the city, every man to his tent. Then Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.
Now Joab was over all the army of Israel, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and over the Pelethites,
Adoram was over the men subject to forced labor, Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was the recorder,
Sheva was scribe, and Zadok and Abiathar were priests,
and Ira the Jairite was chief minister to David.

footnotes.content: A troublemaker's trumpet cuts through the moment—and so many follow. I've watched how a grievance, well-announced, finds ready ears. The kingdom fractures not because the cause was just, but because restless hearts were waiting for permission to scatter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: See how Judah cleaves to David while the north breaks away. Faithfulness isn't always the majority choice. What matters is that the king's own tribe follows him from exile back to the throne—a small anchor in the storm.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David returns home and confines his concubines to perpetual widowhood—neither divorcing them nor taking them back. It's a cruel mercy, the cost of his own sin catching up. Absalom's rebellion left scars that linger in the lives of those caught in the wreckage.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David calls on Amasa to gather the men of Judah. Here's a king still learning to delegate, still trusting men who may not prove reliable. The old impatience is in his voice—three days to rally an army.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Amasa delays, and David's hope grows thin. A king waiting for a general who tarries knows the sting of it—delay looks like betrayal when the kingdom bleeds. Sometimes the slowest servants are those with divided loyalties.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David fears Sheba more than Absalom, his own son. Perhaps a kingdom-wide fracture terrifies him more than family rebellion—one was personal, this one is systemic. He turns to Abishai with the old urgency: pursue, do not delay.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab leads out the loyal troops—the Cherethites and Pelethites, David's foreign mercenaries (the word itself, Cherethites, echoes the Crete-men who formed his standing guard). These are the king's truest servants, the ones paid to stand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At the great stone in Gibeon—a landmark standing for generations—Amasa finally appears. But Joab's sword falls from its sheath 'as he went along.' Notice: the sword slips loose, almost by accident, almost inevitable. Evil men often arrange their evil so it looks unplanned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab greets Amasa like a brother, taking his beard to kiss him. It's the kiss of death disguised as affection. How many treacheries hide behind familiar warmth? The Lord teaches us to test the spirits.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One stroke, and Amasa dies on the road. Joab kills with almost clinical precision—a single, purposeful wound. It's murder dressed up as duty, and the blood spills on the highway for all to see. Evil doesn't hide; it merely calls itself necessity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A young man shouts allegiance to rally the troops. After murder, the machinery keeps turning—the trumpet sounds again, and soldiers forget Amasa's body to follow Joab. Power and loyalty are simpler than justice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Amasa wallows in blood on the highway, and people stop—horrified or afraid, who knows? Someone carries him off the road and covers him with a garment. There's an odd dignity in that small act, that unnamed person honoring the dead while the war moves on.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Once the body is gone from sight, the people forget it entirely. They stream after Joab like sheep. Out of sight, out of mind—that's the way of crowds. We are all capable of that forgetting when the cause seems righteous.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab pursues through all the tribes to Abel and Beth Maacah—real places, real names, a geography of pursuit. The Berites gather around Sheba like water flowing downhill. He has become a symbol now, not a man.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They cast up a mound against Abel's walls and begin battering them down. It's methodical, relentless. How many cities have fallen this way—not in an hour, but in the patient, brutal work of siege and collapse?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A wise woman cries out from the city walls. She sees what the men do not: that this siege will destroy a city of peace-keepers. Sometimes wisdom wears a woman's voice, crying from a wall that no one listens to until the very last moment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab comes near and answers her—'I am.' She hears him, a commander willing to listen for just a moment. In that small opening, a woman's wisdom finds its chance to speak.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The woman invokes an ancient saying: 'They shall surely ask counsel at Abel.' Abel was known for seeking and giving wisdom. She appeals not to force, but to the city's reputation—a place where problems are solved by counsel, not swords.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She pleads that Abel is 'peaceable and faithful' and calls the city 'a mother in Israel.' The language is tender, almost maternal. She reminds Joab that what he destroys is not an enemy camp but a keeper of peace—one that belongs to the covenant people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab's reply is quick: 'Far be it from me that I should swallow up or destroy.' He says he does not seek to destroy the city—only to catch the rebel. In that moment, wisdom and military necessity seem to find an accord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab names Sheba plainly: a man of Ephraim who lifted his hand against the king. The condition is simple: deliver him, and the siege ends. The woman accepts the bargain, and in that exchange, Abel's fate pivots on one head.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The woman goes to 'all the people in her wisdom'—and they obey her. They cut off Sheba's head and cast it to Joab over the wall. One woman's counsel turns a city's fate in an instant. The trumpet sounds again, and the army disperses.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab is over all the army of Israel. Benaiah, over the Cherethites and Pelethites—David's foreign guard. The administrative list begins, marking the true hierarchy. After the blood and chaos, structure returns.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Adoram over forced labor, Jehoshaphat as recorder—these are the men who run the kingdom's machinery. Every one named, every one with a post. Authority is distributed and remembered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sheva as scribe, Zadok and Abiathar as priests. The spiritual and administrative blend—word-keepers and God's servants side by side. The kingdom's order depends on both the pen and the altar.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ira the Jairite served as chief minister—a faithful friend whose name endures in the record. Readers today hear an echo in these lists: the Lord remembers the names of those who serve faithfully, even when the world forgets. Our work is seen, written in Heaven's records.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
